claim: Response inhibition is among the core constructs of cognitive control.
source: Response inhibition is among the core constructs of cognitive control.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field of cognitive control research.

claim: Successful inhibition results in the lack of a behavioral response, making response inhibition difficult to quantify from overt behavior.
source: It is notoriously difficult to quantify from overt behavior, since the outcome of successful inhibition is the lack of a behavioral response.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the measurement challenge inherent in studying inhibition.

claim: The stop signal reaction time (SSRT) is the most common measure of action stopping.
source: Currently, the most common measure of action stopping, and by proxy response inhibition, is the model-based stop signal reaction time (SSRT) derived from the stop signal task.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field, supported by established knowledge.

claim: Partial response electromyography (prEMG) has been introduced as a complementary physiological measure to capture individual stopping latencies.
source: Recently, partial response electromyography (prEMG) has been introduced as a complementary physiological measure to capture individual stopping latencies.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature introducing this measure.

claim: prEMG refers to muscle activity initiated by the go signal that declines after the stop signal before accumulating to a full response.
source: PrEMG refers to muscle activity initiated by the go signal that plummets after the stop signal before its accumulation to a full response.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that describes what prEMG is.

claim: The prEMG peak latency is better suited than SSRT to investigate brain mechanisms of action stopping.
source: Whereas neither the SSRT nor the prEMG is an unambiguous marker for neural processes underlying response inhibition, our analysis indicates that the prEMG peak latency is better suited to investigate brain mechanisms of action stopping.
evidence: This claim is based on the analysis presented in the current study.

claim: SSRTs are slower in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
source: SSRTs are slower in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, drug abuse, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Tourette syndrome among others (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2015; Wylie et al., 2013; Yaniv et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: SSRTs are slower in patients with obsessive compulsive disorder.
source: SSRTs are slower in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, drug abuse, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Tourette syndrome among others (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2015; Wylie et al., 2013; Yaniv et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: SSRTs are slower in patients with drug abuse.
source: SSRTs are slower in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, drug abuse, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Tourette syndrome among others (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2015; Wylie et al., 2013; Yaniv et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: SSRTs are slower in patients with schizophrenia.
source: SSRTs are slower in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, drug abuse, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Tourette syndrome among others (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2015; Wylie et al., 2013; Yaniv et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: SSRTs are slower in patients with Parkinson's disease.
source: SSRTs are slower in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, drug abuse, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Tourette syndrome among others (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2015; Wylie et al., 2013; Yaniv et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: SSRTs are slower in patients with Tourette syndrome.
source: SSRTs are slower in patients with attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, drug abuse, schizophrenia, Parkinson's disease, and Tourette syndrome among others (Jahanshahi et al., 2015; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014; Snyder et al., 2015; Wylie et al., 2013; Yaniv et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: SSRT estimations may be unreliable in many practical settings.
source: However, accumulating evidence suggests that SSRT estimations may be unreliable in many practical settings (Bissett et al., 2021b; Bissett and Logan, 2014; Matzke et al., 2017; Skippen et al., 2019; Verbruggen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to recent research.

claim: The stop signal task has been used in more than 7000 publications in recent years.
source: The stop signal task is among the most common experimental tasks used to study inhibition, with more than 7000 publications using the task in the last years (Verbruggen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: In the stop signal task, participants react to a go signal with a button press but must inhibit this response when a stop signal appears after a variable delay.
source: The principle of the task is very simple: participants react repeatedly to a go signal with a button press but need to inhibit this response when a stop signal appears after the go signal with a variable delay (stop signal delay, SSD).
evidence: This is a description of the standard stop signal task procedure.

claim: The SSRT estimation is based on the independent race model (or horse race model).
source: The SSRT estimation is based on the independent race model (or horse race model), in which go and stop processes independently race against each other, and whichever process wins this race, determines whether a planned action will be executed or not (Band et al., 2003; Logan and Cowan, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational papers on the horse race model.

claim: In the independent race model, go and stop processes independently race against each other.
source: The SSRT estimation is based on the independent race model (or horse race model), in which go and stop processes independently race against each other, and whichever process wins this race, determines whether a planned action will be executed or not (Band et al., 2003; Logan and Cowan, 1984).
evidence: This is a description of the independent race model, supported by citations.

claim: The theoretical basis of the independent race model is well established.
source: The theoretical basis of the model is well established and an extension of this model also has biological plausibility (Boucher et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research on the model's biological plausibility.

claim: SSRT estimates may be inaccurate due to extensive slowing of go responses.
source: However, recent work indicates that SSRT estimates may be inaccurate in many practical cases, for example due to extensive slowing of go responses (Verbruggen et al., 2013), violations of the independence assumptions at short SSDs (Bissett et al., 2021b), or failures to initiate the stop process (Skippen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research on SSRT accuracy.

claim: SSRT estimates may be inaccurate due to violations of the independence assumptions at short SSDs.
source: However, recent work indicates that SSRT estimates may be inaccurate in many practical cases, for example due to extensive slowing of go responses (Verbruggen et al., 2013), violations of the independence assumptions at short SSDs (Bissett et al., 2021b), or failures to initiate the stop process (Skippen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research on SSRT accuracy.

claim: SSRT estimates may be inaccurate due to failures to initiate the stop process.
source: However, recent work indicates that SSRT estimates may be inaccurate in many practical cases, for example due to extensive slowing of go responses (Verbruggen et al., 2013), violations of the independence assumptions at short SSDs (Bissett et al., 2021b), or failures to initiate the stop process (Skippen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to research on SSRT accuracy.

claim: The proposition to use prEMG peak latency as an indicator of stopping speed originated independently in two different laboratories.
source: The proposition to use the peak latency of the prEMG as an indicator of an individual's stopping speed seems to have originated independently in two different laboratories (Atsma et al., 2018; Raud and Huster, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to two independent studies.

claim: Raud and Huster measured prEMG peak latency to be about 150 ms in a selective stop signal task.
source: Raud and Huster used surface EMG from thumb muscles in a selective stop signal task and measured the prEMG peak latency to be about 150 ms, which was significantly shorter than the corresponding SSRT of about 200 ms.
evidence: This claim is based on data from a cited study.

claim: Raud and Huster found the SSRT to be about 200 ms in their selective stop signal task.
source: Raud and Huster used surface EMG from thumb muscles in a selective stop signal task and measured the prEMG peak latency to be about 150 ms, which was significantly shorter than the corresponding SSRT of about 200 ms.
evidence: This claim is based on data from a cited study.

claim: Atsma et al. reported a prEMG offset latency at 165 ms using intramuscular recordings during reaching movements.
source: Atsma et al. used intramuscular recordings of the upper-limb muscle during reaching movements. They reported a prEMG offset latency (the time-point when muscle activity returned to the baseline level) at 165 ms, compared with an SSRT of 244 ms.
evidence: This claim is based on data from a cited study.

claim: Atsma et al. reported an SSRT of 244 ms in their reaching movement task.
source: Atsma et al. used intramuscular recordings of the upper-limb muscle during reaching movements. They reported a prEMG offset latency (the time-point when muscle activity returned to the baseline level) at 165 ms, compared with an SSRT of 244 ms.
evidence: This claim is based on data from a cited study.

claim: Both Raud and Huster and Atsma et al. showed that the EMG-derived stopping latency was much faster than the model-based SSRT.
source: While their methods and goals were different, both studies showed that the EMG-derived stopping latency was much faster than that of the model-based SSRT.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from two cited studies.

claim: Earlier work identified that muscle activity can be stopped at any time before the movement is completed.
source: Earlier work identified that muscle activity can be stopped at any time before the movement is completed, and additionally focused on the time-courses of different electrophysiological measures, that is EMG, electrocardiography, and electroencephalography (EEG; de Jong et al., 1990; Jennings et al., 1992; van Boxtel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to earlier research.

claim: Earlier studies identified the motor cortex as a site of inhibition.
source: These studies identified the motor cortex as a site of inhibition, yet they showed that the peripheral nervous system is affected as well.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from cited earlier studies.

claim: Earlier studies showed that the peripheral nervous system is affected by inhibition.
source: These studies identified the motor cortex as a site of inhibition, yet they showed that the peripheral nervous system is affected as well.
evidence: This claim is based on findings from cited earlier studies.

claim: Trials with prEMG roughly correspond to the middle part of the go-RT distribution.
source: For instance, trials with prEMG seem to roughly correspond to the middle part of the go-RT distribution, indicating that these trials have a relatively fast go process that nonetheless is slow enough to be suppressed by the stop process (de Jong et al., 1990; van Boxtel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to earlier research.

claim: The occurrence of prEMG is dependent on the stop signal delay (SSD).
source: Furthermore, the occurrence of the prEMG is dependent on the SSD, as prEMG frequency declines and its amplitude increases with increasing SSD (Coxon et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to earlier research.

claim: prEMG frequency declines with increasing SSD.
source: Furthermore, the occurrence of the prEMG is dependent on the SSD, as prEMG frequency declines and its amplitude increases with increasing SSD (Coxon et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to earlier research.

claim: prEMG amplitude increases with increasing SSD.
source: Furthermore, the occurrence of the prEMG is dependent on the SSD, as prEMG frequency declines and its amplitude increases with increasing SSD (Coxon et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to earlier research.

claim: EMG in unsuccessful stop trials may be affected by the stop process.
source: Interestingly, EMG in unsuccessful stop trials may be affected by the stop process as well, as these trials exhibit lower EMG amplitudes, but prolonged motor times (the time between EMG onset and the registered response) compared with standard go responses (van de Laar et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to earlier research.

claim: Unsuccessful stop trials exhibit lower EMG amplitudes compared with standard go responses.
source: Interestingly, EMG in unsuccessful stop trials may be affected by the stop process as well, as these trials exhibit lower EMG amplitudes, but prolonged motor times (the time between EMG onset and the registered response) compared with standard go responses (van de Laar et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to earlier research.

claim: Unsuccessful stop trials exhibit prolonged motor times compared with standard go responses.
source: Interestingly, EMG in unsuccessful stop trials may be affected by the stop process as well, as these trials exhibit lower EMG amplitudes, but prolonged motor times (the time between EMG onset and the registered response) compared with standard go responses (van de Laar et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to earlier research.

claim: The finding that unsuccessful stop trials are affected by the stop signal violates the assumption of independence underlying the independent horse race model.
source: This violates the assumption of independence underlying the independent horse race model, which states that unsuccessful stop trials are drawn from the distribution of fast go responses and should therefore be unaffected by the stop signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited findings and the assumptions of the horse race model.

claim: There is a positive correlation between go-locked prEMG onsets and stop-locked prEMG peak latencies at the level of single stop trials.
source: The dependence of go and stop processes was recently directly shown by Raud et al., 2020a who found a positive correlation between go-locked prEMG onsets and stop-locked prEMG peak latencies at the level of single stop trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: The earlier timing of the prEMG peak latency compared to the SSRT has been replicated in multiple independent studies.
source: The earlier timing of the prEMG peak latency compared to the SSRT has been replicated in a number of independent studies (Hannah et al., 2020; Jana et al., 2020; Raud et al., 2020a; Raud et al., 2020b; Sundby et al., 2021; Tatz et al., 2021; Thunberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple independent studies.

claim: The study analyzed surface EMG recorded over the thumb muscles from 46 healthy young adults.
source: We analyzed surface EMG recorded over the thumb muscles (abductor pollicis brevis) from 46 healthy young adults who performed a standard stop signal task.
evidence: This is a description of the study sample and methods.

claim: The primary task was a choice reaction time task where participants responded to a go signal with a left or right hand button press.
source: The primary task was a choice reaction time task where participants had to respond to a go signal either with a left or right hand button press (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental task, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: In 24% of the trials, a stop signal occurred instructing the participants to stop their response.
source: In 24% of the trials, a stop signal occurred instructing the participants to stop their response.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The full analysis pipeline was applied to a publicly available dataset provided by Jana et al., 2020 to replicate the current results.
source: The full analysis pipeline was additionally applied to a publicly available dataset provided by Jana et al., 2020 to replicate the current results.
evidence: This describes the replication analysis performed in the study.

claim: The main difference between the discovery and replication datasets was the proportion of trials with prEMG of successful stop trials.
source: The main difference between these two datasets was the proportion of trials with prEMG of successful stop trials, which was relatively low (~20%) in the discovery, but higher (~60%) in the replication dataset.
evidence: This is a comparison of the two datasets analyzed in the study.

claim: Stopping accuracies were at 50% in the behavioral results.
source: The behavioral results (Table 1) were in line with previous studies, with stopping accuracies at 50% and an SSRT (integration method with RT replacement for go omissions) of 199 ms.
evidence: This is a report of behavioral data from the study.

claim: The SSRT (integration method with RT replacement for go omissions) was 199 ms.
source: The behavioral results (Table 1) were in line with previous studies, with stopping accuracies at 50% and an SSRT (integration method with RT replacement for go omissions) of 199 ms.
evidence: This is a report of behavioral data from the study.

claim: The SSRT estimated using the BEESTS method was 202 ms.
source: We also estimated behavioral parameters using the Bayesian Ex-Gaussian Estimation of Stop Signal Distribution approach accounting for go and trigger failures (BEESTS; Matzke et al., 2019; Matzke et al., 2013), which resulted in an SSRT of 202 ms (Table 1).
evidence: This is a report of behavioral data from the study using an alternative estimation method.

claim: EMG bursts were detected in 99% of go trials.
source: EMG bursts were detected in 99% of go trials and 98% of unsuccessful stop trials.
evidence: This is a report of EMG detection rates from the study.

claim: EMG bursts were detected in 98% of unsuccessful stop trials.
source: EMG bursts were detected in 99% of go trials and 98% of unsuccessful stop trials.
evidence: This is a report of EMG detection rates from the study.

claim: prEMG was detected in 23% of successful stop trials.
source: PrEMG was detected in 23% of successful stop trials.
evidence: This is a report of prEMG detection rates from the study.

claim: EMG onsets were earlier in unsuccessful stop trials than in go trials.
source: This confirmed that the EMG onsets were earlier in unsuccessful stop trials than in go trials (BF = 1.32 × 1024)
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: prEMG onset latencies were similar to the EMG onset latencies in go trials.
source: and that prEMG onset latencies were similar to the EMG onset latencies in go trials (BF = 0.28).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: The peak amplitudes in successful stop trials were considerably smaller than in go trials.
source: The peak amplitudes in successful stop trials were considerably smaller than in go (BF = 2.77 × 1029) and unsuccessful stop trials (BF = 1.91 × 1027).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: The peak amplitudes in successful stop trials were considerably smaller than in unsuccessful stop trials.
source: The peak amplitudes in successful stop trials were considerably smaller than in go (BF = 2.77 × 1029) and unsuccessful stop trials (BF = 1.91 × 1027).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: EMG amplitudes in unsuccessful stop trials were smaller than those in go trials.
source: Interestingly, EMG amplitudes in unsuccessful stop trials were also smaller than those in go trials (BF = BF = 2.32 × 107), suggesting that the former were affected by stop signal processing despite the registered button press.
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: Unsuccessful stop trials were affected by stop signal processing despite the registered button press.
source: Interestingly, EMG amplitudes in unsuccessful stop trials were also smaller than those in go trials (BF = BF = 2.32 × 107), suggesting that the former were affected by stop signal processing despite the registered button press.
evidence: This is an inference based on the EMG amplitude data.

claim: prEMG peaked at 165 ms after the stop signal when time-locked to stop signal onset.
source: When time-locked to stop signal onset, a very clear prEMG waveform appeared (Figure 1D), which started declining at 165 ms after the stop signal.
evidence: This is a report of EMG timing data from the study, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: EMG in unsuccessful stop trials peaked at 99 ms after the stop signal.
source: A similar decline also occurred in unsuccessful stop trials, although they peaked slightly earlier at 99 ms after the stop signal (BF = 3.47 × 1012).
evidence: This is a report of EMG timing data from the study.

claim: The motor time was longer in unsuccessful stop trials than in go trials.
source: Even though the differences are numerically small (Table 2), the motor time was longer in unsuccessful stop trials than in go trials (BF = 5.94; replicating the finding of van de Laar et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data and replicates a previous finding.

claim: Motor times increased with increasing RTs when go trials were divided into fast, medium, and slow trials.
source: When go trials were divided into fast, medium, and slow trials (see paragraph about the assessment of contextual independence for details on this division), the motor times increased with increasing RTs, so that slow go-trial motor times were equivalent to unsuccessful stop trial motor times (BF = 0.16).
evidence: This is a report of motor time analysis from the study data.

claim: Rise times were shorter in unsuccessful stop trials than in go trials.
source: The absolute rise times were also longer in the replication dataset (ranging between 30 and 60 ms for different conditions), but they were shorter in unsuccessful stop trials than in go trials in both datasets (discovery BF = 1.16 × 106; replication BF = 3.93 × 105).
evidence: This claim is supported by Bayesian hypothesis testing on both datasets.

claim: Go RTs correlated strongly with the SSRTs (r = −0.61, p = 1.62 × 10−5).
source: Firstly, goRTs correlated strongly with the SSRTs (r = −0.61, p = 1.62 × 10−5)
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: Go RTs correlated moderately with the prEMG latencies (r = −0.33, p = 0.027).
source: and moderately with the prEMG latencies (r = −0.33, p = 0.027).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: Go RTs correlated moderately with the prEMG detection frequency (r = −0.35, p = 0.018).
source: Secondly, goRTs correlated moderately with the prEMG detection frequency (r = −0.35, p = 0.018).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: The prEMG peak latency was surprisingly stable across 21 different experiments or conditions, averaging to 158 ms.
source: Despite the large variability of goRTs across the studies (range 246 ms), the prEMG peak latency was surprisingly stable (range 35 ms) and averaged to 158 ms with an average detection frequency of 49% (see Table 3 for more descriptive statistics).
evidence: This is a report of meta-analysis results across multiple studies.

claim: The average prEMG detection frequency across studies was 49%.
source: Despite the large variability of goRTs across the studies (range 246 ms), the prEMG peak latency was surprisingly stable (range 35 ms) and averaged to 158 ms with an average detection frequency of 49% (see Table 3 for more descriptive statistics).
evidence: This is a report of meta-analysis results across multiple studies.

claim: There is a strong negative association between go RTs and SSRTs across studies (b = −2.08, t(19) = −2.65, p = 0.012).
source: The strong negative association between go RTs and SSRTs seen across individuals was also evident across studies (b = −2.08, t(19) = −2.65, p = 0.012)
evidence: This is a report of mixed model analysis across multiple studies.

claim: There is an association between go RTs and prEMG peak latencies across studies (b = −1.33, t(11) = −2.21, p = 0.049).
source: as was the smaller association between the go RTs and prEMG peak latencies (b = −1.33, t(11) = −2.21, p = 0.049).
evidence: This is a report of mixed model analysis across multiple studies.

claim: Studies with faster go RTs reported higher prEMG detection frequencies (b = −2.03, t(15) = −2.96, p = 0.010).
source: Similarly, studies with faster go RTs reported higher prEMG detection frequencies (b = −2.03, t(15) = −2.96, p = 0.010).
evidence: This is a report of mixed model analysis across multiple studies.

claim: Every single study reported a positive correlation between the prEMG and the SSRT with an average correlation of r = 0.64.
source: Interestingly, while every single study reported a positive correlation between the prEMG and the SSRT with an average correlation of r = 0.64 (standard deviation covering the range from 0.44 to 0.78 across studies after Student z- and retransformation; Figure 2D)
evidence: This is a report of meta-analysis results across multiple studies, with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: prEMG detection frequency was not associated with its peak latency across studies (b = 0.14, t(19) = 0.91, p = 0.375).
source: Most importantly, while prEMG detection frequency varied considerably across studies (between 23% and 70% of stop trials), it was not associated with its peak latency (b = 0.14, t(19) = 0.91, p = 0.375).
evidence: This is a report of mixed model analysis across multiple studies.

claim: The different SSRT estimates (integration and BEESTS) were comparable in this dataset (BF = 0.34).
source: In line with the latter, we found the different SSRT estimates to be comparable in this dataset (BF = 0.34).
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing comparing SSRT estimation methods.

claim: Both SSRT estimates (integration and BEESTS) were considerably slower than the prEMG peak latency.
source: Both were considerably slower than the prEMG peak latency (integration BF = 9.6 × 105, BEESTS BF = 2.6 × 109).
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing comparing stopping latency measures.

claim: The integration SSRT correlated moderately with the prEMG peak latency (r = 0.51).
source: Both SSRTs correlated moderately with the prEMG peak latency (integration r = 0.51; BEESTS r = 0.57 for prEMG derived from single trials, but see Box 2 for differences in correlations with different prEMG peak latency estimations).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: The BEESTS SSRT correlated moderately with the prEMG peak latency (r = 0.57).
source: Both SSRTs correlated moderately with the prEMG peak latency (integration r = 0.51; BEESTS r = 0.57 for prEMG derived from single trials, but see Box 2 for differences in correlations with different prEMG peak latency estimations).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: The delay between the prEMG and the SSRT (integration) was 33 ms (sd = 33).
source: Consistent with previous studies, the delay between the prEMG and the SSRT (integration) was 33 ms (sd = 33).
evidence: This is a report of timing difference analysis from the study data.

claim: The delay between prEMG and SSRT did not correlate with the prEMG detection frequency (r = 0.04).
source: This did not correlate with the prEMG detection frequency (r = 0.04).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: The effect of SSD on inhibition functions was significant (df = 3.18, F = 213.91, p < 2 × 10−16).
source: The effect of SSD was significant (df = 3.18, F = 213.91, p < 2 × 10−16), as was the parametric effect of response type (b = 0.07, t = 9.52, p < 2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from the study data.

claim: The parametric effect of response type on inhibition functions was significant (b = 0.07, t = 9.52, p < 2 × 10−16).
source: The effect of SSD was significant (df = 3.18, F = 213.91, p < 2 × 10−16), as was the parametric effect of response type (b = 0.07, t = 9.52, p < 2 × 10−16).
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from the study data.

claim: The interaction term between SSD and response type was significant (df = 1.00, F = 6.795, p = 0.009).
source: Further, the interaction term was significant (df = 1.00, F = 6.795, p = 0.009), as the difference between detecting a button press compared to an EMG response was larger at smaller SSDs.
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from the study data.

claim: prEMG was more common in trials with short SSDs.
source: Since p(EMG|stop) contains p(button press|stop) as well successful stop trials with prEMG, these effects indicate that prEMG was more common in trials with short SSDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GAMM analysis results.

claim: The mean unsuccessful stop trial RTs were shorter than go RTs (BF = 1.53 × 1024).
source: This was true in our data both for RTs (BF = 1.53 × 1024) and EMG onset latencies (BF = 1.32 × 1024).
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: The mean unsuccessful stop trial EMG onset latencies were shorter than go EMG onset latencies (BF = 1.32 × 1024).
source: This was true in our data both for RTs (BF = 1.53 × 1024) and EMG onset latencies (BF = 1.32 × 1024).
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: The mean unsuccessful stop trial RTs were not equivalent to the mean of the left side of the go-RT distribution (mean = 470 ms, sd = 72; BF = 1542).
source: We found that the mean unsuccessful stop trial RTs were not equivalent to the mean of the left side of the go-RT distribution (mean = 470 ms, sd = 72; BF = 1542).
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: The participant-specific medians of the left side of the go-RT distribution were equivalent to the unsuccessful stop trial RTs in the discovery set (BF = 0.53).
source: Here, we did find the participant-specific medians of the left side of the go-RT distribution equivalent to the unsuccessful stop trial RTs in the discovery set (BF = 0.53), but not in the replication dataset (BF = 34,849).
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: The average EMG onset in unsuccessful stop trials was slower than the average EMG onset in fast go trials (BF = 2.67 × 109).
source: The data indicate a deviation from the independence assumption already for the left side of the distribution, as the average EMG onset in unsuccessful stop trials was slower than the average EMG onset in fast go trials (BF = 2.67 × 109).
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: The average prEMG onsets were faster than the corresponding average onset of the middle partition of the go-EMG distribution (BF = 2.17 × 104).
source: Secondly, the average prEMG onsets were faster than the corresponding average onset of the middle partition of the go-EMG distribution (BF = 2.17 × 104), which contrasts the prediction that these should be roughly equivalent.
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: The slow go-EMG onsets occurred later than the prEMG onsets (BF = 2.81 × 1021).
source: Lastly, the slow go-EMG onsets occurred later than the prEMG onsets, as expected (BF = 2.81 × 1021).
evidence: This is a report of Bayesian hypothesis testing on the study data.

claim: Extending the horse race model to the EMG is not applicable.
source: These results indicate that extending the horse race model to the EMG is not applicable and, consequently, estimating the SSRT based on go-EMG distributions should be avoided.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EMG onset analysis results.

claim: prEMG probability decreased with the SSD (df = 1.92, F = 24.28, p = 2.47 × 10−10, R2 = 0.09).
source: As expected, prEMG probability decreased with the SSD (df = 1.92, F = 24.28, p = 2.47 × 10−10, R2 = 0.09).
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from the study data.

claim: EMG onsets increased with increasing SSD (df = 2.60, F = 420.7, p < 2.00 × 10−16, R2 = 0.36).
source: Similarly, we found increased EMG onsets with increasing SSD (df = 2.60, F = 420.7, p < 2.00 × 10−16, R2 = 0.36).
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from the study data.

claim: prEMG peak latencies decreased with SSD (df = 2.29, F = 11.77, p = 9.71 × 10−6, R2 = 0.06).
source: The prEMG peak latencies decreased with SSD (df = 2.29, F = 11.77, p = 9.71 × 10−6, R2 = 0.06), indicating that stopping may be slower at short SSDs.
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from the study data.

claim: Stopping may be slower at short SSDs.
source: The prEMG peak latencies decreased with SSD (df = 2.29, F = 11.77, p = 9.71 × 10−6, R2 = 0.06), indicating that stopping may be slower at short SSDs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GAMM analysis results.

claim: Trial order did not affect prEMG peak latency (df = 1.173, F = 0.11, p = 0.843).
source: We tested this by fitting a GAMM model predicting prEMG peak latency by trial order while controlling for SSD (model R2 = 0.04), but we found no evidence that the trial order would affect prEMG peak latency (df = 1.173, F = 0.11, p = 0.843).
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from the study data.

claim: Trial order did not affect prEMG frequency (df = 1.00, χ2 = 0.87, p = 0.350).
source: We also tested whether the trial order affected prEMG frequency by predicting the existence of prEMG in a given trial from the trial order using logistic regression (while controlling for the SSD), but this model yielded no trial order effects either (df = 1.00, χ2 = 0.87, p = 0.350).
evidence: This is a report of logistic regression analysis results from the study data.

claim: There was a strong positive relationship between onset and peak latencies at the single-trial level (edf = 3.47, F = 1957, p < 2 × 10−16, R2 = 0.72).
source: The data showed evidence for scenario 2 (Figure 7) with a strong positive relationship between onset and peak latencies (estimated degrees of freedom [edf] = 3.47, F = 1957, p < 2 × 10−16, R2 = 0.72).
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from single-trial data, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: There was a small negative association between onset latencies and the AUCs at the single-trial level (edf = 1.00, F = 29.25, p = 7.93 × 10−8, R2 = 0.03).
source: There was also a small negative association between onset latencies and the AUCs (edf = 1.00, F = 29.25, p = 7.93 × 10−8, R2 = 0.03).
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from single-trial data.

claim: There was no relationship between peak latencies and AUCs in the discovery dataset (edf = 1.00, F = 0.09, p = 0.77, R2 < 0.001).
source: In the discovery dataset, there was no relationship between peak latencies and AUCs (edf = 1.00, F = 0.09, p = 0.77, R2 < 0.001), while the replication dataset showed a very small negative association (edf = 1.00, F = 12.96, p = 0.0003, R2 < 0.001).
evidence: This is a report of GAMM analysis results from single-trial data.

claim: There was strong evidence for dependencies between going and stopping at the single-trial level, where delayed going was associated with delayed stopping.
source: As such, there was strong evidence for dependencies between going and stopping at the single-trial level, where delayed going was associated with delayed stopping.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the single-trial analysis results.

claim: The average individual standard deviation of prEMG peak latency was 31 ms (group-level sd = 21).
source: The average individual standard deviation was 31 ms (group-level sd = 21) and varied from 7 to 90 ms.
evidence: This is a report of variability analysis from the study data.

claim: Individual variability in prEMG peak latency correlated moderately with the number of prEMG trials (r = 0.30, p = 0.05).
source: The individual variability in prEMG peak latency correlated moderately with the number of prEMG trials (r = 0.30, p = 0.05), but showed no associations with baseline EMG noise (r = 0.06, p = 0.72) or go-RT variability (r = −0.01, p = 0.94).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: Individual variability in prEMG peak latency showed no associations with baseline EMG noise (r = 0.06, p = 0.72).
source: The individual variability in prEMG peak latency correlated moderately with the number of prEMG trials (r = 0.30, p = 0.05), but showed no associations with baseline EMG noise (r = 0.06, p = 0.72) or go-RT variability (r = −0.01, p = 0.94).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: Individual variability in prEMG peak latency showed no associations with go-RT variability (r = −0.01, p = 0.94).
source: The individual variability in prEMG peak latency correlated moderately with the number of prEMG trials (r = 0.30, p = 0.05), but showed no associations with baseline EMG noise (r = 0.06, p = 0.72) or go-RT variability (r = −0.01, p = 0.94).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: There was a moderate positive correlation between the prEMG variability and the variability of the SSRT calculated using the BEESTS method (r = 0.40, p = 0.01).
source: Lastly, we replicated the moderate positive correlation reported by Jana et al., 2020 between the prEMG variability and the variability of the SSRT calculated using the BEESTS method (r = 0.40, p = 0.01).
evidence: This is a report of correlation analysis from the study data, replicating a previous finding.

claim: The split-half reliability for prEMG onset latency was high (0.94).
source: Using all available trials and participants, we found high reliability for latency measures (0.94 and 0.87 for the prEMG onset and peak latency, respectively) but somewhat lower reliability for the prEMG peak amplitude and AUC (0.51 and 0.48, respectively).
evidence: This is a report of reliability analysis from the study data.

claim: The split-half reliability for prEMG peak latency was high (0.87).
source: Using all available trials and participants, we found high reliability for latency measures (0.94 and 0.87 for the prEMG onset and peak latency, respectively) but somewhat lower reliability for the prEMG peak amplitude and AUC (0.51 and 0.48, respectively).
evidence: This is a report of reliability analysis from the study data.

claim: The split-half reliability for prEMG peak amplitude was lower (0.51).
source: Using all available trials and participants, we found high reliability for latency measures (0.94 and 0.87 for the prEMG onset and peak latency, respectively) but somewhat lower reliability for the prEMG peak amplitude and AUC (0.51 and 0.48, respectively).
evidence: This is a report of reliability analysis from the study data.

claim: The split-half reliability for prEMG AUC was lower (0.48).
source: Using all available trials and participants, we found high reliability for latency measures (0.94 and 0.87 for the prEMG onset and peak latency, respectively) but somewhat lower reliability for the prEMG peak amplitude and AUC (0.51 and 0.48, respectively).
evidence: This is a report of reliability analysis from the study data.

claim: The reliability estimates for prEMG onset latency remained high (above 0.8) regardless of reduction in the number of trials and/or participants.
source: Interestingly, the reliability estimates for prEMG onset latency remained high (above 0.8) no matter the reduction in the number of trials and/or participants.
evidence: This is a report of reliability analysis across different trial counts.

claim: prEMG peak latency reliability increased with the number of trials and reached a plateau around 0.77 after around 13 trials.
source: prEMG peak latency reliability increased with the number of trials and reached a plateau around 0.77 after around 13 trials (with increased confidence intervals as the number of participants decreased).
evidence: This is a report of reliability analysis across different trial counts.

claim: The latency measures of prEMG have overall good reliability.
source: In sum, we conclude that the latency measures of prEMG have overall good reliability, while amplitude-based measures do not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reliability analysis results.

claim: Amplitude-based measures of prEMG do not have good reliability.
source: In sum, we conclude that the latency measures of prEMG have overall good reliability, while amplitude-based measures do not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the reliability analysis results.

claim: An optimal minimal number of trials for prEMG analysis is around 15.
source: While reliability measures are affected by the specifics of each dataset, our data suggest an optimal minimal number of trials to be around 15, and more is always better.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the reliability analysis results.

claim: Excluding participants based on low number of available trials is not strictly necessary and may reduce statistical power.
source: However, the reliability estimates were highest when all participants (even those with less than 10 trials) were included. Thus, excluding participants based on low number of available trials is not strictly necessary and may cause more harm by increasing the group-level standard errors and thereby reducing statistical power.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the reliability analysis results.

claim: Several results indicate incompatibility of the prEMG with the horse race model.
source: Several results from our analysis indicate incompatibility of the prEMG with the horse race model.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple analysis results.

claim: Neither unsuccessful stop trials nor successful stop trials with prEMG matched the corresponding partitions of the go-EMG distributions.
source: On the other hand, neither unsuccessful stop trials nor successful stop trials with prEMG matched the corresponding partitions of the go-EMG distributions.
evidence: This is a summary of analysis results comparing EMG distributions.

claim: The horse race model framework should not be extended to the go-EMG distribution.
source: This indicates that the horse race model framework should not be extended to the go-EMG distribution.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the EMG distribution analysis.

claim: prEMG peak latency varied with the SSD, indicating that stopping latency is not stable.
source: Furthermore, prEMG peak latency varied with the SSD, indicating that stopping latency is not stable.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the SSD analysis results.

claim: The go process and the stop process share about 70% of variance at the single-trial level if the SSD is accounted for.
source: Lastly, the single-trial analysis indicated a major violation of the horse race model independence assumption, as the go process (measured by the go-locked prEMG onset latency) and the stop process (measured by the stop-locked prEMG peak latency) share about 70% of variance if the SSD is accounted for.
evidence: This is a report of single-trial analysis results.

claim: The independent horse race model is not an appropriate approximation of the stopping performance in practice.
source: Together, these results add to the increasing pool of evidence which suggests that the independent horse race model is not an appropriate approximation of the stopping performance in practice.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple analysis results.

claim: The prEMG peak latency occurs earlier than the SSRT.
source: First, the prEMG peak latency occurs earlier than the SSRT.
evidence: This is a summary of findings comparing prEMG and SSRT timing.

claim: The prEMG correlates moderately to highly with the SSRT.
source: Second, the prEMG correlates moderately to highly with the SSRT.
evidence: This is a summary of correlation findings.

claim: The 60ms delay between the prEMG peak latency and SSRT may reflect the final ballistic component of the movement, the point of no return.
source: The 60ms delay between the myographic (prEMG peak latency) and behavioral (SSRT) measures may reflect the final ballistic component of the movement, the so-called point of no return, after which initiated movements are unaffected by any higher-order control mechanism (Osman et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the timing difference, supported by a citation.

claim: The prEMG may reflect the inertia in the neuromuscular system and response device after the prepared movement has been stopped in the cortex.
source: In this case, the prEMG may simply reflect the inertia in the neuromuscular system and response device presiding after the prepared movement has been stopped in the cortex (Gopal and Murthy, 2016; Jana et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: 'Leakage' EMG has been shown to have milder rising slopes compared to normal go-EMG responses.
source: First, such 'leakage' EMG has been shown to have a milder rising slopes compared to the normal go-EMG responses (McGarry and Franks, 2003; McGarry and Franks, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In the current study, the EMG onset slopes were identical for all trial types.
source: In the current study, the EMG onset slopes were identical for all trial types (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a report of EMG slope analysis from the study data, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The SSRT correlates negatively with go RTs, both across individuals in a single study and across different studies.
source: In support of this, the SSRT correlates negatively with go RTs, both across individuals in a single study, as well as across different studies.
evidence: This is a summary of correlation findings from the study and meta-analysis.

claim: The prEMG detection frequency is affected by task characteristics, evidenced by correlations with go RTs.
source: Whereas the prEMG detection frequency is also affected by task characteristics, evidenced by the correlations with go RTs, the primary outcome of interest, the peak latency, is relatively stable across different studies.
evidence: This is a summary of correlation findings from the meta-analysis.

claim: The prEMG peak latency is relatively stable across different studies.
source: Whereas the prEMG detection frequency is also affected by task characteristics, evidenced by the correlations with go RTs, the primary outcome of interest, the peak latency, is relatively stable across different studies.
evidence: This is a summary of meta-analysis findings.

claim: The prEMG peak latency captures action stopping speed and its variability across single trials.
source: In sum, the prEMG peak latency captures action stopping speed and its variability across single trials.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about what prEMG measures.

claim: The SSRT likely captures action stopping to some degree but is further affected by strategic behavioral adaptations and inaccuracies due to violations of the horse race model's assumptions.
source: The SSRT likely captures action stopping to some degree but it is further affected by strategic behavioral adaptations and inaccuracies due to violations of the horse race model's assumptions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about what SSRT measures, based on the study findings.

claim: The prEMG latency distribution is a truncated representation of the distribution of the underlying stopping process.
source: The prEMG latency distribution is a truncated representation of the distribution of the underlying stopping process, lacking trials in which actions were stopped cortically before muscle activation or in which go process was not initiated in the first place.
evidence: This is an inference about the nature of the prEMG distribution.

claim: The prEMG distribution is affected by two interacting processes – action generation and action stopping.
source: The prEMG distribution is thus affected by two interacting processes – action generation and action stopping.
evidence: This is an inference about what influences the prEMG distribution.

claim: Participants and studies with faster RTs produced more prEMG trials, but there was no relationship between the prEMG frequency and peak latency.
source: First, participants and studies with faster RTs produced more prEMG trials, but there was no relationship between the prEMG frequency and peak latency.
evidence: This is a summary of correlation findings from the study and meta-analysis.

claim: The fact that the prEMG distribution is truncated does not invalidate its use as a marker of action stopping.
source: Altogether, the fact that the prEMG distribution is truncated does not invalidate its use as a marker of action stopping, since the peak latencies are relatively stable despite the varying number of trials available for its estimation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the stability of prEMG peak latencies across different trial counts.

claim: Stopping actions may be achieved by different underlying mechanisms across different tasks and within the same task across different trials.
source: However, stopping actions may be achieved by different underlying mechanisms across different tasks, as well as within the same task across different trials.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the nature of stopping mechanisms.

claim: McGarry and Franks, 1997 found that they could differentiate between trials with early and late stopping mechanisms based on the shape of the prEMG rising slope.
source: McGarry and Franks, 1997 designed a stop signal task with untypically short SSDs, and found that they could differentiate between trials with early and late stopping mechanisms based on the shape of the prEMG rising slope (see Box 1 about interrupted response for details), although it has been disputed that the same pattern could result from the differential recruitment times of motor neurons with different sizes (van Boxtel and Band, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: EEG studies have found that prEMG trials show decreased lateralized readiness potentials and increased frontal negativities.
source: Further, EEG studies have found that prEMG trials show decreased lateralized readiness potentials and increased frontal negativities (de Jong et al., 1990; van Boxtel et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increased frontal negativities have been related to awareness of the prEMG in response conflict tasks.
source: Increased frontal negativities have also been related to awareness of the prEMG in response conflict tasks (Ficarella et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The SSRT becomes increasingly unreliable in more complex stop signal tasks and its use is discouraged.
source: While it has been shown that the SSRT becomes increasingly unreliable in more complex stop signal tasks and its use is thus discouraged (Bissett and Logan, 2014), prEMG can still be recorded in such task settings (Raud et al., 2020a; Raud and Huster, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: prEMG can be recorded in complex stop signal task settings.
source: While it has been shown that the SSRT becomes increasingly unreliable in more complex stop signal tasks and its use is thus discouraged (Bissett and Logan, 2014), prEMG can still be recorded in such task settings (Raud et al., 2020a; Raud and Huster, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: EMG can be recorded in any task that requires overt responses and in tasks that require more complex movements activating several muscle groups.
source: Further, (pr)EMG is not limited to the stop signal task, but can be recorded in any task that requires overt responses, as well as tasks that require more complex movements activating several muscle groups (Tao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: One study found that the prEMG peaked significantly later in the go/no-go task than in the stop signal task.
source: For example, one study using this approach found that the prEMG peaked significantly later in the go/no-go task than in the stop signal task. This was also paralleled by differences in cortical activity, suggesting that these tasks may recruit different mechanisms (Raud et al., 2020b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Tatz et al., 2021 showed that EMG activity declines after any infrequent salient stimulus.
source: Similarly, Tatz et al., 2021 showed that EMG activity declines after any infrequent salient stimulus, highlighting the interdependence between attentional capture and inhibitory control constructs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: prEMG decline unequivocally indicates stopping of muscle activity.
source: On the one hand, prEMG decline unequivocally indicates stopping of muscle activity, so it is safe to presume that the peak latency represents the latency of action stopping.
evidence: This is a logical inference about what prEMG decline indicates.

claim: The actual mechanisms that cause EMG decline cannot be derived from prEMG alone.
source: On the other hand, the actual mechanisms that cause this EMG decline cannot be derived from prEMG alone.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prEMG as a measure.

claim: Several studies have investigated whether stopping of specific muscle activity could be caused by the activation of antagonist muscles and found that agonist stopping occurs before antagonist activation.
source: Several studies have investigated whether stopping of specific muscle activity could be caused by the activation of antagonist muscles and found that agonist stopping occurs before antagonist activation; thus, the former cannot be caused by the latter (Atsma et al., 2018; Corneil et al., 2013; Goonetilleke et al., 2012; Goonetilleke et al., 2010; Scangos and Stuphorn, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: It is unlikely that prEMG represents initial subthreshold go activations, as such stimulus-locked responses are typically <100 ms after stimulus onset.
source: It is also unlikely that prEMG represents initial subthreshold go activations, as such stimulus-locked responses are typically <100 ms after stimulus onset (Pruszynski et al., 2010), while prEMG onsets are closer to 300–500 ms.
evidence: This is an inference based on timing comparisons, supported by a citation.

claim: prEMG is a useful and reliable measure of action stopping.
source: Based on the synthesis of previous work together with a comprehensive analysis of prEMG characteristics in an independent dataset, we conclude that prEMG is a useful and reliable measure of action stopping.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study findings and literature review.

claim: prEMG is not limited to specific muscles, stimulus modalities, or task contexts.
source: PrEMG is not limited to specific muscles, stimulus modalities, or task contexts, so it provides a comparative physiological measure for a range of different scenarios.
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of prEMG, based on the literature review.

claim: The SSRT and prEMG should not be used interchangeably, but rather complementarily.
source: Even though there are some similarities between the SSRT and the prEMG, these two measures should not be used interchangeably, but rather complementarily.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: The SSRT is founded on assumptions that are not always met in empirical data.
source: Yet, it is founded on assumptions that are not always met in empirical data, and it seems to be more strongly affected by behavioral strategies than the prEMG.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study findings and literature review.

claim: prEMG is directly observable and provides action stopping latencies at a single-trial level.
source: In contrast, prEMG is directly observable and provides action stopping latencies at a single-trial level.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of prEMG as a measure.

claim: Neither the SSRT nor the prEMG peak latency is an unambiguous marker of response inhibition in the brain.
source: Importantly, neither the SSRT nor the prEMG peak latency is an unambiguous marker of response inhibition in the brain, but since the prEMG is directly observable, it has stronger potential for guiding research on brain mechanisms underlying action stopping.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the interpretation of both measures.

claim: prEMG has stronger potential than SSRT for guiding research on brain mechanisms underlying action stopping.
source: Importantly, neither the SSRT nor the prEMG peak latency is an unambiguous marker of response inhibition in the brain, but since the prEMG is directly observable, it has stronger potential for guiding research on brain mechanisms underlying action stopping.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparative advantages of prEMG.

claim: Data were analyzed from 46 healthy young adults (mean age = 23.7, sd = 5.5, 30 females, 3 left-handed).
source: Data were analyzed from 46 healthy young adults (mean age = 23.7, sd = 5.5, 30 females, 3 left-handed).
evidence: This is a description of the study sample.

claim: Initially, data were collected from 52 participants, but four were discarded due to technical issues and two were discarded as statistical outliers.
source: Initially, data were collected from 52 participants, but four were discarded due to technical issues with the response device and another two were discarded as statistical outliers (above two interquartile ranges) based on EMG onset and peak latencies.
evidence: This is a description of the data exclusion criteria.

claim: The study was conducted in accordance with the Helsinki declaration and was approved by the internal review board of the University of Oslo.
source: The study was conducted in accordance with the Helsinki declaration, and was approved by the internal review board of the University of Oslo (ref. 1105078).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: In total, there were 684 go trials and 216 stop trials, equally distributed between left- and right-hand trials.
source: In total, there were 684 go trials and 216 stop trials, equally distributed between left- and right-hand trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The initial SSD was set to 250 ms, and then increased or decreased by 50 ms following successful and unsuccessful stop trials, respectively.
source: The initial SSD was set to 250 ms, and then increased or decreased by 50 ms following successful and unsuccessful stop trials, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the adaptive tracking procedure.

claim: Two surface EMG electrodes were placed on the skin above the abductor pollicis brevis in parallel to the belly of the muscles on each hand.
source: Two surface EMG electrodes were placed on the skin above the abductor pollicis brevis in parallel to the belly of the muscles on each hand using bipolar Ag/Ag-Cl montages.
evidence: This is a description of the EMG recording setup.

claim: The EMG recordings were performed with a sampling rate of 5000 Hz.
source: The recordings were performed using a BrainAmp ExG extension for bipolar recordings (Brain Products GmbH, Germany) with an online low-pass filter of 1000 Hz, a sampling rate of 5000 Hz, and a 0.5 µV resolution.
evidence: This is a description of the EMG recording parameters.

claim: The EMG signal was bandpass filtered between 20 and 250 Hz using a second-order butterworth filter.
source: The EMG signal was bandpass filtered between 20 and 250 Hz using a second-order butterworth filter and resampled to 500 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the EMG preprocessing steps.

claim: Trials were rejected if the average baseline activity was larger than 100 μV.
source: Trials were rejected at this stage if the average baseline activity was larger than 100 μV (across all participants, this led to the rejection of 206 trials, i.e., roughly 0.5 %).
evidence: This is a description of the trial rejection criteria.

claim: EMG bursts were identified in a trial if any data point exceeded a threshold of 1.2 standard deviation units.
source: EMG bursts were identified in a trial if any data point exceeded a threshold of 1.2 (in standard deviation units, taking into account all trials).
evidence: This is a description of the EMG burst detection method.
